# AI writing patterns

<!-- This file is generated from `human-eyes/scripts/patterns.json`. Edit the JSON and regenerate via `python3 human-eyes/scripts/build_patterns_md.py --write`. -->

79 patterns to detect and fix, organised by category. Each identifier is a category letter and a position within that category, so a new pattern joins its category without renumbering anything else. Each entry has words to watch, a brief description of the problem, and a before/after example, and carries a **Detection** marker stating whether the pattern is enforced by a programmatic check or left to manual / agent-judgement reading. 8 patterns also carry a **Below threshold** marker: when one of those checks runs and passes, it still reports how many instances it counted.
_meta.evidence_body:
Use source strength when deciding severity. The ruleset should surface clusters of suspicious writing behaviours, not claim that one phrase proves AI authorship.

**Strong empirical backbone:**

- Kobak / Science Advances and the `llm-excess-vocab` dataset support lexical spike detection at corpus level. Scope: 15,103,888 complete English PubMed biomedical abstracts, 2010-2024, with word occurrence measured as binary per abstract rather than as per-document density. Use vocabulary as density and clustering evidence, not as one-word proof, and never as universal banned words: the paper states its method cannot identify individual abstracts processed by an LLM, and its proposed extension to grants, peer review, news, social media, and general prose is unvalidated follow-up. Source: https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab
- Juzek and Ward's "Why does ChatGPT delve so much?" supports a narrow scientific-abstract vocabulary signal. It is credible for excess-word lists but not for confident document-level claims. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.11385
- GPTZero's 2026 paper supports the architecture: hierarchical signals, granular findings, adversarial testing, and transparent mixed evidence. It does not add a prose-style rule by itself. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13042
- Stanford HAI's detector-bias reporting supports warnings over accusations, especially for non-native English writers. Use process evidence and user review rather than detector-style verdicts. Source: https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-detectors-biased-against-non-native-english-writers

**Useful but tentative style sources:**

- GPTZero's AI Vocabulary page is useful as a phrase list, but its own framing separates vocabulary scanning from AI-probability scoring. Use all 100 public table rows only as clustering signals. Source: https://gptzero.me/ai-vocabulary
- Shreya Shankar's AI Writing essay is one of the strongest craft references: bad sentence subjects, orphaned demonstratives, empty paragraph endings, over-bulleting, flat rhythm, low information density, vagueness, and fluency without understanding. These directly support the self-audit and several programmatic checks. Source: https://www.sh-reya.com/blog/ai-writing/
- OpenAI's April 2025 GPT-4o sycophancy rollback documents sycophantic model behaviour as a shipped incident class. Source: https://openai.com/index/sycophancy-in-gpt-4o/

**Domain and provenance signals:**

- Walsh, Preus, and Gronski support poetry-specific manual checks: constrained uniformity, rhyme/quatrain defaults, first-person plural overuse, and mood-word clusters. Keep this genre-specific. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15299
- Clarkesworld reporting supports fiction as a submission/provenance problem and a manual craft-audit area. Source: https://www.npr.org/2023/02/24/1159286436/ai-chatbot-chatgpt-magazine-clarkesworld-artificial-intelligence
- Futurism's Sports Illustrated reporting supports journalism and review-provenance checks: fake bylines, fake bios, AI headshots, affiliate product-review sludge, undisclosed generated content, and byline laundering. Source: https://futurism.com/sports-illustrated-ai-generated-writers

**2026 operating stance:**

- Em dashes are still used by human writers, but in publication-ready plain prose they are now a strong AI-style signal. Treat them as strong warnings. They must be removed at every depth (Balanced and All); preserve only when the source genuinely uses them stylistically and the preservation is disclosed.
- The best signals are clusters: GPTZero/Kobak vocabulary density, contrived contrast laundering, empty endings, vague demonstrative starts, placeholder residue, sycophantic assistant residue, unrequested headings/lists/Unicode flair, paragraph uniformity, generic email closers, and fake citations or provenance artifacts.

category_preambles.Sensory and atmospheric: These patterns are especially common in descriptive, creative, and reflective writing. AI reaches for sensory language but, having no physical experience, attaches it to abstractions.
category_preambles.Voice and register: These patterns concern what AI **removes** from writing — stance, personality, specificity — rather than what it adds. LLMs systematically strip argumentative commitment and deplete personal voice even in minimal edits.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Emojis attached to headings and bullet points as decoration. They add nothing the words beside them do not already say. These emojis are among those G4 flags.

examples.before:
:rocket: **Launch:** The product ships in Q3
:white_check_mark: **Next steps:** Schedule the follow-up
examples.after: The product ships in Q3. The next step is to schedule the follow-up.
fix: The next step is to schedule the follow-up

what_it_looks_like.example:
## Getting Started 🚀

Install the app and sign in.

## Pricing 💰

Plans start at five dollars.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Remove the emoji and let the words stand. If the decorated fragments were doing the work of sentences, rewrite them as prose.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep emojis in registers where they are standard, like chat messages and social posts.
_extra_entries.description: Emojis decorating headings and bullet points.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Flattery in place of an answer: the question is called great, the point excellent, before any substance arrives. These lines are among those D1 flags.

examples.before: You're absolutely right that shipping costs drove the loss. Excellent point about the fuel surcharge; it was the largest single line item.
examples.after: Shipping costs drove the loss. The fuel surcharge was the largest single line item.

what_it_looks_like.example: You're absolutely right, the second draft reads much better.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Cut the compliment and answer the substance. When the sentence carried a real point, keep only the point: "You're absolutely right that costs rose" becomes "Costs rose".
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep praise inside quoted speech; a quoted character or correspondent keeps their words, and text inside double quotation marks is not read. Praise that names what was good and moves on to the substance is ordinary writing; the check flags only the listed lines.
_extra_entries.description: People-pleasing praise directed to the reader.

what_it_looks_like.prose: One sense described in the words of another: grief gets a taste, a voice gets a colour. The forced kind attaches a sensation to something no one perceived.

examples.before: The morning after the funeral had a metallic taste, and her sister's voice on the phone was the colour of faded curtains.
examples.after: The morning after the funeral felt wrong, and her sister's voice on the phone sounded flat.

what_it_looks_like.example: Her grief tasted of copper, and the silence had the texture of wet wool.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Rewrite the phrase around something a person in the scene could notice. When nothing observed lies behind it, cut it and name the feeling plainly.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep crossed senses that are deliberate and anchored: literary prose built on something the writer really perceived, and everyday idiom like a loud shirt or a sharp cheese. The test is whether a specific experience sits behind the phrase.
_extra_entries.description: One sense described using words for a different sense.

what_it_looks_like.prose: The metaphor fits any subject: swap in a different noun and it still works.

examples.before: Every chord is a puzzle piece that finally clicks into a song.
examples.after: Each chord shape takes practice until it comes without thinking.
problem: a puzzle piece that finally clicks into a song
fix: takes practice until it comes without thinking

what_it_looks_like.example: Grief is like an ocean, with waves that pull you under when you least expect them.
problem: like an ocean, with waves that pull you under

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Replace the metaphor with a concrete detail about the subject itself.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep a metaphor that comes from a specific scene or names a property the surrounding text actually uses.
_extra_entries.description: Bland generic metaphors that could apply to anything.

what_it_looks_like.prose: One register held from the first sentence to the last. Human writing drifts; unbroken consistency is the tell.

examples.before: Our community garden has grown steadily this season. Volunteers have contributed their time each weekend, and the new compost system has improved soil quality. We are grateful for everyone's continued support and look forward to another productive month.
examples.after: The garden has grown steadily this season. Volunteers have been out every weekend, and the compost system is doing its job: the soil is better. We're grateful, truly, for everyone who keeps showing up.
fix: We're grateful, truly, for everyone who keeps showing up

what_it_looks_like.example: Building a reading habit is simpler than most people assume. The key is consistency, and anyone can develop it. Start with ten minutes a night and let the routine do the work.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Break the single tone at least once with an aside or a looser sentence. Put the break where the content invites it.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep a locked register where the genre demands one: contracts, safety instructions, reference documentation. A steady tone there is the form doing its job.
_extra_entries.description: Generic bland register, or abrupt changes in register.

what_it_looks_like.prose: A detail that sounds personal but comes from genre convention rather than anyone's life.

examples.before: There is something about the way a handwritten letter feels in your hands: the weight of the paper, the smudge of ink. It reminds you that someone took the time to think of you.
examples.after: A handwritten letter tells you that someone sat down and took the time to think of you.
problem: There is something about the way
the weight of the paper, the smudge of ink
fix: someone sat down and took the time to think of you

what_it_looks_like.example: Think of the way your coffee smells before the first sip, or the morning light on your kitchen table.
problem: the way your coffee smells before the first sip
the morning light on your kitchen table

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Swap the detail for one from a particular life, one no other writer could have produced. When you have no real detail, cut the passage instead of inventing one.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep a generic sensory detail when the writing is openly about a shared experience and claims no one's in particular: a guided meditation, an ad built around a familiar morning. It fails only when it poses as personal testimony.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Every side gets equal treatment and the writer's own conclusion disappears. E4 covers added optimism; this pattern covers removed opinion.

examples.before: There are strong arguments on both sides of the remote work debate. The productivity studies that measured output found remote workers doing as well or better. That said, in-person work has its own advantages, and the right choice likely depends on each team's context.
examples.after: Remote work holds up. The productivity studies that measured output found remote workers doing as well or better.
problem: That said, in-person work has its own advantages
likely depends on each team's context

what_it_looks_like.example: There are compelling arguments on both sides, and the best approach depends on each team's context.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Restore the position: state the conclusion outright, and keep a counterargument only where the piece answers it.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep neutrality where the genre requires it: news reporting, a survey of open questions, a brief written to lay out both sides. Balance there is the assignment.
_extra_entries.description: Removing opinions and positions on rewrite.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Faults that only exist against one genre's conventions: a dialogue tag avoiding `said` in fiction, fake personalisation in a marketing email. The same move passes in another genre.

examples.before: "You never told me he was coming," she exclaimed. "I didn't think it mattered," he responded quietly.
examples.after: "You never told me he was coming," she said. "I didn't think it mattered," he said quietly.

what_it_looks_like.example: "We should leave before dark," she remarked. "The road is worse than you remember," he responded.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Repair the fault by its genre's own standard. Verify the citation in a paper. Change `remarked` to `said` in fiction. Swap fake personalisation for a real detail in an email.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep a convention broken on purpose: a dialogue tag other than "said" used for effect, an email that starts warm because the sender is warm, a poem that chooses its form.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Two statements that cannot both be true, or numbers that do not add up. Machine drafts fit each sentence to its neighbours, so far-apart passages disagree.

examples.before: The pilot ran at three depots and every driver completed the new handover form. At Dandenong, about half the drivers never opened it.
examples.after: The pilot ran at three depots. At Dandenong, about half the drivers never opened the new handover form.
examples.note: The source material supports the Dandenong figure, so the every-driver claim is the one cut.
problem: every driver completed the new handover form
about half the drivers never opened it
fix: about half the drivers never opened the new handover form

what_it_looks_like.example: Of the applications, 61 per cent were approved, 32 per cent were deferred, and 14 per cent were declined.
problem: 61 per cent were approved, 32 per cent were deferred, and 14 per cent were declined

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Check both halves against the source material and correct the one that is wrong. If nothing settles it, keep the claim the text supports and cut the other. Never adjust the numbers just to make the contradiction disappear.

evidence_sources.contribution: Its Appendix A shows that contradictions, unsupported statistics, and arithmetic errors hand a reader checkable evidence where style signals cannot; the examples are qualitative model outputs, not controlled estimates.

_extra_entries.description: Inherent contradictions of fact that cannot both be true.

what_it_looks_like.prose: A disclaimer volunteered where nothing called for one: results vary, the approach will not suit everyone. D2 covers hedges about missing information; this pattern covers every other uninvited caveat.

examples.before: The team moved the nightly export to 03:00 and cut failures from eleven a month to one. Every environment differs, and what worked here carries no guarantee elsewhere. The remaining failure was a timeout on the largest table.
examples.after: The team moved the nightly export to 03:00 and cut failures from eleven a month to one. The remaining failure was a timeout on the largest table.
problem: Every environment differs, and what worked here carries no guarantee elsewhere

what_it_looks_like.example: Of course, results vary from person to person, and this approach may not suit every reader.
problem: Of course, results vary from person to person, and this approach may not suit every reader

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Cut the caveat and let the claim stand at its actual strength.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep a caveat tied to a stated risk, an acknowledged limit, or a convention of the genre: a limitations section in a research paper, safety documentation, medical and legal writing. A factual qualification with a real basis is part of the claim and stays.
_extra_entries.description: Unsolicited disclaimers that qualify or hedge.

what_it_looks_like.prose: A beginner explanation in a text that has already said who it is for: a runbook for on-call engineers pausing to define latency.

examples.before: This runbook is for the on-call SRE rotation. Before the failover procedure, recall that latency is the time a request takes to travel from client to server and back. Treat p99 latency above 400 ms as a paging condition.
examples.after: This runbook is for the on-call SRE rotation. Treat p99 latency above 400 ms as a paging condition. The failover procedure follows.
problem: recall that latency is the time a request takes to travel from client to server and back

what_it_looks_like.example: Before we look at the failover steps, remember that latency means the time a request takes to travel from one system to another.
problem: remember that latency means the time a request takes to travel from one system to another

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Cut the explanation the stated audience already has and spend the space on the part they came for.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep basic definitions in a text written for mixed readers: a release note read by engineers and buyers, or a handbook used by first-week and tenth-year staff, defines terms for its widest reader. Where the text never states or implies its audience, there is nothing to mismatch, and defining terms is the fair default.
_extra_entries.description: Beginner-level explanations in a text otherwise written for experts.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Every section makes the same run of moves: a claim, its support, a tidy close, repeated under each heading. G6 covers the headings and labels; this pattern covers the moves inside the sections.

examples.before:

Billing is what fills the support queue
is the change worth making first

what_it_looks_like.example:
## Pricing

Pricing is where most teams stumble first, because a supplier can double its rates midway through a contract and eat the whole budget. Work the likely rise into the plan before anyone signs.

## Support

Support is where most teams stumble next, because a supplier can take six weeks to answer a routine ticket during an outage. Work the delay into the plan before anyone signs.

## Contracts

Contracts are where most teams stumble last, because a supplier can bury an auto-renewal clause on page nine. Work the exit cost into the plan before anyone signs.
problem: Pricing is where most teams stumble first
Support is where most teams stumble next
Contracts are where most teams stumble last

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Rework the section that least fits the shared shape: start it on the evidence, or end it unresolved.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep the fixed shape in reference entries and templated reports, where a set order lets a reader skip to the part they need.
_extra_entries.description: Repetitive and formulaic sections and paragraphs.

what_it_looks_like.prose: The text describes current behaviour by comparison with an old version the reader cannot see.

examples.before: # Note: this now returns a list of spans instead of a tuple.
examples.after: # Returns a list of spans.

what_it_looks_like.example: The parser now returns a list of spans instead of a tuple.

_extra_entries.how_to_fix: Replace the comparison with a statement of current behaviour. Move history worth keeping into a changelog or release note.
_extra_entries.when_to_keep: Keep change narration in writing whose job is to compare versions: changelogs, release notes, migration guides, deprecation notices. A release note that described only current behaviour would have failed at its job.
_extra_entries.description: Documentation or comments that report what changed instead of stating what is.

no-ai-vocabulary-clustering.description: Clusters of words over-used by AI.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Words that machine writing overuses, such as `delve` and `vibrant`, sitting close together in one stretch of text. Each is ordinary alone; several together is the tell.

examples.before: The festival will showcase local artists, foster community ties, and enhance the town's vibrant reputation.
examples.after: The festival will present local artists, build community ties, and improve the town's reputation.

what_it_looks_like.example: Her thesis delves into the intricate interplay between housing costs and wages in coastal cities.

no-ai-vocabulary-clustering.how_to_fix: Swap each listed word for the plain word it stands in for: `delve into` becomes `look at`, `enhance` becomes `improve`. If no plain word fits, cut the word.
no-ai-vocabulary-clustering.when_to_keep: Keep a listed word that carries its literal meaning, like a landscape in a painting or a tapestry on a wall, and thin out the listed words around it instead.

editor_guidance.why: Words machine writing overuses are gathered close together here, and the cluster reads as generated text.
editor_guidance.fix: Swap each listed word for the plain word it stands in for, or cut it when no plain word fits.
editor_guidance.keep: Keep a listed word used literally, like a real tapestry on a wall, and thin the listed words around it.

paragraph-cluster.why: This paragraph packs {matchCount} of the listed words together, which is where the clustering shows.

document-family-pair.why: The word family {family} recurs alongside other listed families across the document.

editor_action_policy.reason: A cluster requires revising several context-dependent words rather than one meaning-preserving swap.
