no-nominalisation-rate.description: High rate of nouns built from verbs and adjectives.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Nouns built from verbs and adjectives, such as `implementation` and `assessment`, crowding the sentences. Each hides an action inside an abstract noun.

examples.before: The implementation of the new procurement system required extensive coordination across departments. Following the completion of the initial assessment, the team began the documentation of existing workflows, with particular attention to the identification of redundancies. The expectation was that automation would deliver a reduction in processing time, but the realisation of these benefits depended on the standardisation of supplier records. Resistance from regional offices slowed the adoption of the platform, and the persistence of manual workarounds undermined the accuracy of early reports. Management responded with the establishment of a governance board, whose recommendations included additional training and the simplification of approval chains.
examples.after: When we rolled out the new procurement system, teams across every department had to work together closely. After the first review, the team wrote up how work currently flowed and looked hard for steps that repeated each other. We expected the software to make orders faster to process, but that only came true once every supplier record followed the same format. The regional offices were slow to take up the platform, and because staff kept using their old manual workarounds, the early reports could not be trusted. So we set up a small governance board, which told us to train more staff and cut the number of people who had to approve each order.
fix: wrote up how work currently flowed
set up a small governance board

what_it_looks_like.example: The consultation on the new road closed last week. Most people who wrote in are against the placement of the site gate across from the school, and many also doubt the measurement of noise, since the meter sat too far from the bend to catch the worst of the morning trucks. The council says the assessment will be finished well before October. A commitment to fund a safer crossing might calm some of the anger, but the mood at the last meeting was sour, and the room did not trust a word of the announcement about the new commitment to consultation.

no-nominalisation-rate.how_to_fix: Turn the noun back into its verb: `the implementation of the change` becomes `we changed it`.
no-nominalisation-rate.when_to_keep: Keep a nominalisation that names a specific document rather than an act, such as `the settlement` or `the assessment`.

editor_guidance.why: Nouns built from verbs run at a high rate, which buries the actions they stand for.
editor_guidance.fix: Turn the noun back into its verb: 'the implementation of the change' becomes 'we changed it'.
editor_guidance.keep: Keep a nominalisation that names a specific document rather than an act, such as 'the settlement'.

no-that-relative-rate.description: High rate of 'that' clauses where the noun does the acting.

what_it_looks_like.prose: A `that` clause after a noun, saying what the noun does: `the dog that bit me`. One is ordinary grammar; sentence after sentence carrying one is the tell.

The chart that shows regional sales loaded slowly, and the filter that controls the date range reset itself whenever the page refreshed. We fixed the query that caused the delay and rewrote the code that handles the filter. The release that followed was smoother, and the managers that check the dashboard each morning now open a page that loads in under two seconds, even on hotel wifi.
examples.after: The weekly numbers dashboard went live last month. Its builders worked with the owner of the reporting pipeline, and the first week's feedback was blunt. what_it_looks_like.example: The shed that flooded last winter has finally been cleared, and the boxes went up to the barn that sits higher on the lane, out of reach of the stream. Most of what we saved was tools, along with the bench that belonged to my grandfather and the crates of jars that survived the mud. The pump that failed in the storm now has a float switch that shuts it off when the water drops below the intake. The insurance covered the roof but not the freezer, so the meat was a loss, and next autumn we will stack anything of value onto pallets before the rain sets in.

no-that-relative-rate.how_to_fix: Cut the clause or fold it into the noun: `the report that describes the failure` becomes `the failure report`.
no-that-relative-rate.when_to_keep: Keep a clause that tells the reader which one you mean: `the copy that went to print` picks one copy out from several.

editor_guidance.why: Clauses like 'the dog that bit me', where the noun does the acting, run at a high rate, a pattern machine prose leans on.
editor_guidance.fix: Cut the clause or fold it into the noun: 'the report that describes the failure' becomes 'the failure report'.
editor_guidance.keep: Keep a clause that picks one thing out from several: 'the copy that went to print'.

editor_action_policy.reason: Recasting a subject-relative clause requires grammatical restructuring.

no-participial-clause-rate.description: High rate of '-ing' phrases adding a second action to a sentence.

what_it_looks_like.prose: An `-ing` clause adding a second action to a sentence: `Stuffing his mouth with cookies, Joe ran out the door`. Machine prose attaches one to sentence after sentence.

what_it_looks_like.example: She spent the morning on the harbour wall, watching the boats come in with the first catch. The buyers stood in a row by the scales, stamping their feet against the cold and shouting bids over the gulls. Her father worked the winch, hauling crate after crate onto the wet stones until the hold was empty. By ten the market floor was awash and the last van pulled away up the hill, carrying ice and mackerel for the shops in town. She bought two crabs from the smallest boat on the wall and walked home along the same wall, eating bread from her coat pocket.

no-participial-clause-rate.how_to_fix: Give the clause its own subject and verb: `Leaning on the rail, she watched the boats` becomes `She leaned on the rail and watched the boats`. If it adds nothing, cut it.
no-participial-clause-rate.when_to_keep: Keep a clause that shows two actions happening at once when the timing is the point. A few across a page read as ordinary variety; the problem is the density.

editor_guidance.why: Clauses built on an '-ing' verb hang a second action onto sentences at a high rate here.
editor_guidance.fix: Give the clause its own subject and verb, or cut it if it adds nothing.
editor_guidance.keep: Keep a clause that shows two actions happening at once when the timing is the point.

editor_action_policy.reason: A finite-clause rewrite requires the intended actor and tense.

what_it_looks_like.prose: A passive verb drops the actor: `the proposal was rejected` names nobody. One is ordinary English; machine drafts stack them until nobody does anything.

examples.before: The annual report was completed in March and was submitted to the board before the deadline. what_it_looks_like.example: The village hall was built in 1911 and was extended twice before the war, and the roof was damaged so badly in the January storm that the repairs were finished only last month. During the work, the old stage curtains were found folded under the floor, wrapped in newspaper from 1953. no-passive-voice-rate.how_to_fix: Say who did it, or move the doer in front of the verb when the sentence already names them: `the figures were checked` becomes `two clerks checked the figures`.
no-passive-voice-rate.when_to_keep: Keep a passive when the actor is unknown or beside the point: `the window was smashed overnight`. A scattering of passives across a page is ordinary English; the finding means the rate has climbed. Set phrases built on adjective-like participles, such as `is based on`, `was interested in`, and `is known for`, are not counted, so leave them as they are.

editor_guidance.why: Passive verbs run at a high rate, hiding who does what.
editor_guidance.fix: Say who did it: 'the figures were checked' becomes 'two clerks checked the figures'.
editor_guidance.keep: Keep a passive when the actor is unknown or beside the point: 'the window was smashed overnight'.

The committee discussed it at length in September, and it was agreed that it should be reviewed again in the new year before it is extended to the second site.

what_it_looks_like.example: The bread oven came with the house, and it took us a full year to learn its moods, because it heats unevenly unless the coals are raked twice, and it holds the warmth long after the fire dies. We nearly bricked it up in the first winter, but the neighbour talked us out of that, and now it earns its keep every Saturday. I light it at dawn and feed it split beech until nine, then sweep it clean and load the first trays of dough. By noon it has done the loaves, the buns, and whatever the kids have shaped from the scraps of the first trays.

no-it-pronoun-rate.how_to_fix: Name the thing `it` stands for, or cut the empty frame around it: `It is worth noting that costs rose` becomes `Costs rose`.
no-it-pronoun-rate.when_to_keep: Keep `it` where the referent sits close by and the sentence stays clear: `the pump sticks in cold weather, so run it for a minute first`. The possessive `its` is not counted.

editor_guidance.why: The pronoun 'it' appears unusually often, which blurs what each sentence is about.
editor_guidance.fix: Name the thing 'it' stands for, or cut the empty frame: 'It is worth noting that costs rose' becomes 'Costs rose'.
editor_guidance.keep: Keep 'it' where the referent sits close by and the sentence stays clear.

editor_action_policy.reason: Replacing 'it' requires the real referent or a deliberate impersonal construction.

no-latinate-verb-rate.description: High rate of formal verbs standing in for plainer verbs.

what_it_looks_like.prose: Formal Latin-derived verbs where plain ones belong: `obtain` for get, `commence` for start. A draft using one every few sentences reads like a form letter.

The portal will also handle renewals, and reminder letters will show the date on which the current permit runs out. Anyone who cannot get into the portal should telephone the office, where staff will help with the form and post out a paper copy on request. The council expects the change to save money and plans to tell every household before the old system shuts down in the autumn.

editor_guidance.why: Formal Latinate verbs stand in for plainer ones at a high rate, stiffening the prose.

editor_guidance.keep: Keep a listed verb when it is the precise word: a court terminates a lease.

examples.before: The organisation's transformation programme necessitated comprehensive restructuring across administrative departments. Preliminary evaluations demonstrated measurable improvements in productivity indicators, although employee satisfaction assessments revealed persistent concerns regarding workload distribution and professional development opportunities. The transformation committee subsequently published revised strategic objectives, emphasising accountability, transparency, and continuous improvement throughout the enterprise. Regional managers received supplementary guidance concerning implementation timelines, budgetary allocations, and anticipated milestones for the forthcoming financial period.

Early checks showed that work got done faster, though staff still felt they had too much to do and too few ways to move up. The board then set out fresh goals: own your work, be open, keep getting better. Local managers got extra notes on dates, money, and the goals for the year ahead.

examples.before: The initiative's success depends on sustained alignment between strategic priorities and organisational capabilities. Effective governance requires clarity of purpose, consistency of approach, and a shared understanding of intended outcomes.
